title_content.content: Pd/Brønsted Acid Co-catalyzed Dehydrative Coupling of Propargylic Alcohols with Diarylphosphine Oxides

paragraph_content.content: Zhaoqiang Chen and Hui Qian*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2025, 27, 522−527
Metrics & More

ABSTRACT: An eficient dehydrative coupling of propargylic alcohols with diarylphosphine oxides to construct tetrasubstituted allenylphosphoryl compounds in the presence of a Pd/Brønsted acid co-catalyst has been developed. As a benefit from the use of a Brønsted acid, this reaction could perform under mild conditions with excellent yields, accommodating a wide range of functional groups. The potential utility of this method has also been demonstrated.

remains a topic of enduring significance due to the diverse applications in pharmaceutical science,<sup>1</sup> materials chemistry,<sup>2</sup> and organic chemistry.<sup>3</sup> Introducing phosphorus atoms into organic molecules could result in substantial modifications to their chemical and physical properties, rendering phosphination a commonly employed eficient method for generating innovative compounds. Allenyl phosphine oxides, specific types of P-functionalized unsaturated compounds, have garnered considerable interest in recent years due to their distinctive allenic structure and phosphorus functionality, which embedded them with unique reactive and biological activities.<sup>4−7</sup> Therefore, increasing attention has been focusing on the advancement of novel methodologies to acquire phosphorus-substituted allenes. The traditional approach for their preparation mainly relies on the Horner−Mark rearrangement reaction, which underwent an intermediate of propargyl phosphate (Scheme 1a).<sup>8</sup> Although delivering the desired allenylphosphoryl compounds, it sufered from toxic and unstable reagents as well as a limited substrate scope. To overcome these issues, transition-metal (TM)-catalyzed coupling of propargylic derivatives with readily available and stable secondary phosphine oxides has been called in for the synthesis of such compounds (Scheme 1b).<sup>9</sup> The direct dehydrate C−P coupling of propargylic alcohols is the most straightforward and eficient strategy; however, the C−O bond is much more inert and less reactive. Therefore, Lewis acid catalysts had been applied in such transformations with a high temperature (Scheme 1c).<sup>10</sup> Inspired by previous work,<sup>11</sup> a catalytic amount of Brønsted acid could facilitate the hydroxy group to form a transient leaving group and could be further converted to construct the C−C bond in the presence of a palladium catalyst. Here, we reported the dehydrative C−P coupling of propargylic alcohols with

could also aford the desired product with lower yields (entries 2−4 in Table 1); however, all of the tested Pd(II) catalysts failed to catalyze the coupling reaction (entries 5 and 6 in Table 1). Further screening indicated that room temperature gave a better result (entries 7 and 8 in Table 1). Next, we set out to investigate the solvent efect. The yield increased to 80% when MeCN was applied (entry 9 in Table 1). Ethers, such as methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), tetrahydrofuran (THF), and dioxane, were not efective (entries 10−12 in Table 1). Dichloromethane (DCM) was found to be optimal and provided a 92% nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) yield of product 3aa (entry 13 in Table 1). Controlling experiments showed that phosphoric acid and palladium are necessary for the reaction (entries 14 and 15 in Table 1). The reaction aforded a 40% yield only in the absence of DPEphos (entry 16 in Table 1). Thus, the optimized reaction conditions entailed the use of 4 mol %
\mathrm { P d } ( \mathrm { P P h } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 } ,
6 mol % DPEphos, and 5 mol % (PhO) POOH in DCM at room temperature for 16 h.

With the optimized conditions in hand, we next explored the reaction scope (Scheme 2). Propargylic alcohols bearing a wide range of aryl groups with electron-donating (1b−1e) and electron-withdrawing (1f−1i) substituents all reacted smoothly with diphenylphosphine oxide 2a, forming the corresponding tetrasubstituted allenylphosphoryl products (3ba−3ia) in decent to excellent yields. It is worth mentioning that the steric efect seems to have no impact because substrates containing a methyl group at the ortho, meta, and para positions of the phenyl group all produced the intended products (3ba−3da) in significant yields. The reaction of 2- (naphthalen-2-yl)oct-3-yn-2-ol also performed well under the standard conditions, giving an 88% yield of allene product 3ja. Heteroaryl groups, such as furyl and thienyl, also furnished target products 3ka and 3la in decent yields. The

Meanwhile, reactions of other diarylphosphine oxides, including halides (F and Br) and trifluoromethyl substituents, had also been studied, providing allene possessing diferent kinds of phosphoryl groups with good yields (3ab−3ad). Finally, we also performed the C−P coupling reaction with H-phosphonates. Diethyl phosphite 2e exhibited a low reactivity, and only 10% yield of product 3ae could be supplied. When compound 2e was replaced with cyclic H-phosphonate 2f, the corresponding products 3af and 3wf could be obtained with satisfactory results.

To gain insight into the mechanism, kinetic studies were conducted and showed that the reaction was first-order in the catalyst and Brønsted acid (Scheme 4). These data indicated

chart_caption.content: that both palladium catalyst and phosphoric acid were essential for facilitating the conversion of propargylic alcohol to allene. These findings were also consistent with the results of the controlling experiments (entries 14 and 15 of Table 1). On the basis of the above experimental results and previous reports,<sup>11,12</sup> a possible catalytic cycle was proposed in Scheme

in which propargylic alcohol 1 would be activated by Brønsted acid to yield oxonium intermediate I, which would easily undergo an anti-oxidative addition with palladium(0) to deliver allenyl palladium intermediate II. Then, a ligandexchange process would happen between intermediate II and in situ-generated tautomeric P(III). Subsequent reductive elimination formed the desired product and regenerated the palladium(0) species.

paragraph_content.content: In summary, we have developed an eficient strategy for the dehydrative coupling to produce the corresponding tetrasubstituted allenylphosphoryl products. The key to our protocol mainly relies on the introduction of Brønsted acid to enhance the leaving ability of the hydroxyl group, which makes the reaction work well under mild conditions with better substrate compatibility. Further studies are currently ongoing in our laboratory.
